'''Robert Works Fuller''' (October 26, 1936 – July 15, 2025) was an American [[Physics|physicist]], educator and social reformer. He was president of [[Oberlin College]] 1970–1974, where he championed diversity and curricular reform.<ref>{{citation|url=https://oberlin.libraryhost.com/repositories/2/resources/87|title=Robert Works Fuller Biographical Sketch|publisher=Oberlin College Archives|last=Archives Staff|date=1995}} Retrieved July 3, 2025.</ref> He then worked for citizen diplomacy during the [[Cold War]], helped found the [[Hunger Project]], which worked to end world hunger, travelled and wrote widely advocating societies free from "Rankism", rank-based discrimination.

Fuller was a Fellow of the [[World Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Robert Fuller|url=https://worldacademy.org/author/worldacademy/|access-date=2023-11-21|website=World Academy of Arts and Sciences|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
Fuller was born in [[Summit, New Jersey]], on October 26, 1936, the son of Willmine Works Fuller and physical chemist [[Calvin Souther Fuller]], the co-inventor of the solar battery. He enrolled in Oberlin at the age of fifteen, and, when he had taken all the available courses in physics, left after three years to enter [[Princeton University]],  where he was a friend and collaborator of [[John Archibald Wheeler]],{{sfnb|Fuller|2025|}} and protégé of neurologist Peter Putnam.<ref name="Gefter 2025">{{cite web | last=Gefter | first=Amanda | title=Finding Peter Putnam | website=Nautilus | date=June 17, 2025 | url=https://nautil.us/finding-peter-putnam-1218035/ | access-date=June 18, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Putnam Fuller 1964">{{cite web |last2=Fuller|first2=Robert|last1=Putnam|first1=Peter| title=Outline of a Functional Model of the Nervous System, Putnam/Fuller 1964 | website=The Peter Putnam Papers | date=October 30, 1970 | url=https://www.peterputnam.org/outline-of-a-functional-model-of-the-nervous-system-putnam/fuller-1964 | access-date=June 18, 2025}}</ref>  He did graduate study there from 1955 to 1957, at the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École normale supérieure]] in Paris, a year at the [[University of Chicago]] in economics, before returning to Princeton for an M.A., receiving his Ph.D. in physics in 1959. In that year he married Ann Lackritz.{{sfnb|Archives Staff|1995}}

He taught at [[Columbia University]] as an assistant professor (1965–66), where he co-authored the book ''Mathematics of Classical and Quantum Physics''. In the following years he did research at the Center for Advanced Studies at [[Wesleyan University]] and [[Teachers College]] of Columbia University. At the Battelle Seattle Research Center Seattle, Washington, he worked on support programs for school drop-outs and students who did not live up to their potential.

==Trinity College==
Fuller was Dean of the Faculty and Professor of Physics at [[Trinity College (Connecticut)|Trinity College]] in Hartford, Connecticut from  1968 to 1970, at that time an all-male school. Among his responsibilities were opening admission and integration of women students and making the college attractive to minority students.{{sfnb|Archives Staff|1995}} When Fuller announced his resignation in May 1970, President Lockwood said the college had "benefitted immeasurably from Dr, Fuller’s wisdom, ability, and energy", and the campus newspaper called Fuller "perhaps the most articulate spokesman for many of the College’s recent innovations", such as coeducation, the new curriculum, the judicial system, and praised his "willingness to innovate on a campus with a conservative faculty and a history of uninspired mediocrity".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Fuller, Dean of Faculty, Resigns; Credited with Curriculum Change|journal= The Trinity Reporter | volume=1 |number= 1 |date=May 1970 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/community.31571845?seq=4|jstor=stable/community.31571845?seq=4 }} Accessed 18 July 2025.</ref>

==Oberlin College president==
The mounting social unrest of the 1960s, and Fuller's commitment to educational reform led Oberlin College in 1970, to make him its tenth president, succeeding [[Robert K. Carr]]. At age 33 Fuller became one of the youngest college presidents in the country.{{sfnb|Archives Staff|1995}} His Oberlin presidency was a turbulent time on campus and in higher education generally. He told a reporter that Oberlin was outstanding because "it was founded by a bunch of Christians who took literally from the Bible certain dictums which said that all people are created equal and therefor you couldn’t not have women and you couldn’t not have Blacks." The faculty, he continued, is "politically and socially very liberal", but needs "a greater tolerance for experimentation". The curriculum had not changed in twenty years, he added. The faculty ran the internal affairs of the college, and students and administration had no say in a lot of things, which tended to perpetuate the status quo.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Heschel |first=H. Susannah |title=Visiting Oberlin College |journal= The Trinity Tripod |date= 9 May 1972|url= https://jstor.org/stable/community.29898466 |volume=70 |number=31}}</ref>

===Structural reform and student life===
Fuller established a Education Commission made up of faculty, administration, and students to consider basic structural change in the curriculum and calendar.<ref>{{citation|first=Robert W. |last=Fuller |title=A Year of Decisions |journal= Oberlin Alumni Magazine |volume=67 |date= September–October 1971|pages=5–7, 21 |url=}}</ref>  The Commission recommended a new calendar of four 7-week sessions, six for course work and the seventh for evaluation and counselling. The proposed schedule would  permit students to study two subjects instead of four, allow two additional sessions and create year-round operation. The year-round operation would lead to an increase in the size of the student body and faculty. Among the other recommendations were a high ratio of students to faculty in some areas in order to allow a low ratio in others; a series of lectures for large student audiences, for which only a light amount of reading woud be required, encouraging students to take courses in a wider range of topics; an increase in independent work; decreasing requirements and increasing student responsibility, that is, to drop requirements as to subject matter, language, physical education, and departmental major.<ref>Donald R. Reich, “[https://archive.org/details/oberlinalumnimag1971ober_h6v1/page/9/mode/1up?view=theater Educational Opportunity at Oberlin: The Preliminary Report of the Education Commission],” Oberlin Alumni Magazine    9-12</ref>

The college drew national attention for offering the option of co-ed dorms. ''[[Life Magazine]]'' ran a cover story in November 1970 that called the co-ed dorms a "marked success".  Fuller  told the magazine "we operate on good old American basic: the majority of students rule and determine their own life style."<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Life Magazine |first=Karen |last=Thorsen|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2FMEAAAAMBAJ&q=Robert+Fuller&pg=PA32 |title=Co-ed Dorms: An Intimate Revolution in Campus Life |date=20 November 1970 |page=39}}</ref>

===Women and minority programs===
Fuller also established a Commission on the Status of Women, tripled the enrollment of minorities, and increased support for the African Studies program started under President Carr.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://oberlinreview.org/19867/news/reflecting-on-50-years-of-africana-studies/|title= Africana Studies and A-House Established
|journal= The Oberlin Review |date=15 November 2019 |last=Koeninger |first=Alice}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://oberlinreview.org/19867/news/reflecting-on-50-years-of-africana-studies/|title= Africana Studies Program Created Against Backdrop of National Activism|journal= The Oberlin Review |date=15 November 2019 |last= Carpenter |first=Nathan }}</ref>

===Arts===
Although the Conservatory was strong, Oberlin had not emphasized theater. Fuller recruited [[Herbert Blau]] to head the Inter-Arts Program, which included the actor [[Bill Irwin]] and the director [[Julie Taymor]]. He encouraged The Oberlin Dance Collective.<ref>[https://shadowproof.com/2013/12/13/belonging-a-memoir-the-oberlin-years/ Belonging: A Memoir] "The Oberlin Years."</ref>

===Sports: The "Oberlin Experiment"===
In what has been called the "[[Jack Scott (sportswriter)#The "Oberlin Experiment"|Oberlin Experiment]]", he recruited and hired [[Jack Scott (sportswriter)|Jack Scott]], activist and writer on the sociology of sports, as chairman of the physical education department and athletic director.  Scott, in turn, recruited and hired the first four African-American athletic coaches at a predominantly white American college or university, including [[Tommie Smith]], Gold Medalist sprinter from the [[1968 Summer Olympics]] in [[Mexico City]], and a woman for women's sports. Scott and Fuller were interviewed on campus by [[Howard Cosell]] and appeared on primetime television to talk about these changes they were seeking.<ref>{{citation|first= Anne|last= Trubek|title= The Oberlin Experiment|date = 14 December 2007| journal = The Smart Set| url= https://www.thesmartset.com/article12140702/ |ref=none}}</ref>
Fuller supported Scott's moves to make sports more democratic and part of college life. To help eliminate the distinction between so-called major and minor sports, he did away with admission charges to all Oberlin sporting events and gave team members power over the selection of coaches and their training rules.<ref>{{citation |title=Overhaul at Oberlin |journal=Time Magazine |date=29 January 1973 |volume= 101|number= 5 |url= https://search.ebscohost.com/login.aspx?direct=true&db=f6h&AN=53812781&site=eds-live&scope=site}}</ref>

===Resignation===
In November 1973, Fuller informed the Board of his resignation, to be effective February 2, 1974, making his tenure the shortest of any Oberlin president. He told local media that he had "achieved what I was asked to do". He listed cultural diversity and increased opportunities for women as major achievements during his tenure. Many changes had taken place in the curriculum, system of evaluation, and flow between the College and the Conservatory, but the dispute over governance made further progress difficult.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Fuller Resigning As President February 2 |journal=Oberlin Alumni Magazine |volume = 69 |number= 6|date= December 1973 |pages=2–3 |url= https://archive.org/details/oberlinalumnimag1973ober_o6g1/page/2/mode/2up}}</ref>

He was succeeded by [[Emil C. Danenberg]], dean of the Conservatory. In 2019, the ''Oberlin Review'' looked back and quoted a faculty member who said Fuller's brief tenure was so unnerving that the college "spent the next decade quietly knitting itself together". However, the Review added, "while many faculty felt threatened by what they viewed as administrative overreach, not all faculty members opposed Fuller"  and many students saw merit in his proposals.<ref>{{citation|date= 4 October 2019|first= Nathan |last= Carpenter |title= Carmen Ambar and Bobby Fuller: Contrasting Two Presidencies|journal=Oberlin Review|url=https://oberlinreview.org/19518/opinions/carmen-ambar-and-bobby-fuller-contrasting-two-presidencies/}}</ref>

==Ventures in social reform==
Fuller had a longstanding interest in social and economic reform. In 1971 on a visit to India, Fuller had witnessed the famine caused by war with Pakistan; the war was a catalyst for the emergence of [[Bangladesh]] as an independent nation.{{sfnb|Family|2025}} With the election in the United States of President [[Jimmy Carter]], he began a campaign to persuade the new leader to end world hunger. In 1977, Fuller joined [[Werner Erhard]] and singer [[John Denver]] in forming [[The Hunger Project]], which worked to generate a consensus on ending world hunger.<ref>"[https://wernererhardfoundation.org/hunger.html The Hunger Project]," History of the Werner Erhard Foundation, 1973-1991.</ref> His June 1977 meeting with Carter in the [[Oval Office]] helped lead to the establishment of the Presidential Commission on World Hunger.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Presidential Commission on World Hunger|url=http://www.jimmycarterlibrary.org/library/fed_records.phtml|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Jimmy Carter Library|language=en-US}}</ref>

During the 1970s and 1980s, Fuller traveled frequently to the [[Soviet Union]], working as a citizen-scientist to improve superpower relations during the [[Cold War]]. This led to the creation of the Mo Tzu Project, a group of [[Citizen diplomacy|citizen-diplomats]] traveling the world seeking citizen-to-citizen understanding to create sustainable peace.<ref>{{Cite web
| url = http://www.context.org/iclib/ic04/
| title = The Foundations of Peace
| website = Context Institute
| date = September 19, 2011
| language = en-US
| access-date = 2016-02-26
}}</ref>  His frequent travel partner, [[Robert Cabot]], funded these travels and became his patron for some fifteen years.{{sfnb|Salamon|2004|}} Fuller also participated in the creation of the nonprofit global corporation Internews,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Internews|url= http://www.internews.org/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Internews|language=en-US}}</ref> which promoted democracy via free and independent media. Fuller served as its chairman, working with [[Kim Spencer]], [[David M. Hoffman]] and [[Evelyn Messinger]] (founders of [[Internews]]), Alia Johnson, Robert Cabot, and John Steiner, among others. In 1982, Fuller appeared in the PBS documentary ''Thinking Twice About Nuclear War.''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Thinking Twice About Nuclear War.|url=https://vimeo.com/180973927|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Vimeo|date=31 August 2016|language=en-US}}</ref>

With the [[collapse of the USSR]], Fuller's turn as a citizen-diplomat came to a close. Reflecting on the different roles he had played, he came to understand that he had, at various times, enjoyed the status of a "somebody" while at other times he had embraced the position of a "nobody". His experiences in "Nobodyland" led him to identify [[rankism]]—a term he coined, and defined as the abuse of the power inherent in rank.{{citation needed|date=August 2023}}

In 2003, Fuller published ''Somebodies and Nobodies: Overcoming the Abuse of Rank'' (New Society Publishers). The book led a group in Virginia to set up the Dignitarian Foundation. He published a sequel that focused on building a dignitarian society, titled ''All Rise: Somebodies, Nobodies, and the Politics of Dignity'' (Berrett-Koehler, 2006).  The concept of the "[[politics of dignity]]" builds on his broader analysis of rankism, arguing that many contemporary conflicts—whether in workplaces, families, institutions, or nations—stem less from material deprivation than from systematic violations of personal dignity. A politics of dignity, in Fuller’s account, seeks to reform institutions so that authority is exercised without humiliation, enabling individuals to participate without fear of being demeaned or rendered invisible.
Ultimately, he envisions a civic order in which recognition, respect, and protection from rank-based discrimination form the basis of a more just and stable society.<ref>{{cite book
 | last=Fuller
 | first=Robert W.
 | title=All Rise: Somebodies, Nobodies, and the Politics of Dignity
 | publisher=Berrett-Koehler
 | location=San Francisco
 | year=2006
 | isbn=9781576753859
}}</ref> In 2008, Fuller and co-author Pamela A. Gerloff released an 86-page "action-oriented guide" titled ''Dignity for All: How to Create a World Without Rankism''.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Fuller
 | first = Robert W.
 | author2=Pamela A. Gerloff
 | year = 2008
 | title = Dignity for All: How to Create a World Without Rankism
 | publisher = Berrett-Koehler Publishers
 | isbn = 978-1-57675-789-5
 | no-pp = true
 | page = back cover
}}
</ref>

Fuller frequently spoke at universities, conferences, and social policy organizations. Notable engagements{{citation needed|date=March 2021}} include:
* National Conference on Dignity for All, Dhaka, Bangladesh<ref>{{Cite web|title=National Conference on Dignity for All|url= http://civicbd.org/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Civicbd|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* World Academy of Arts and Sciences<ref>{{Cite web|title=World Academy of Arts and Sciences|url= http://www.worldacademyforum.org/Agenda%20for%20World%20Academy%20Forum%20on%20the%20Future%20of%20Higher%20Education%20-%20Oct%202-3,%202013.pdf|access-date=2021-05-01|website=World Academy Forum|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* Institute for Social and Economic Change, Bangalore, India<ref>{{Cite web|title=Seminars Given by Visitors|url=http://www.isec.ac.in/seminars-given-visitors.htm|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Institute for Social and Economic Change|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* Center for Therapeutic Justice, Williamsburg, Virginia
* National Association of Graduate-Professional Students (Keynote Speaker)<ref>{{Cite web|title=2013 Regional Conference|url=http://nagps.org/members/regions/western/regional-conference/2013-regional-conference/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=National Association of Graduate-Professional Students|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society, Berkeley, CA<ref>{{Cite web|title= Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society|url=http://diversity.berkeley.edu/haas-institute|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Haas Institute for a Fair and Inclusive Society|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* Berkeley Carroll School (Visiting Writers Program)<ref>{{Cite web|title=Berkeley Carroll School (Visiting Writers Program)|url=http://www.berkeleycarroll.org/news/article/index.aspx?LinkId=8611&ModuleId=315|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Berkeley Carroll School|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington 
* [[Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology]], Australia
* Maison des Sciences de l’Homme, Paris<ref>{{Cite web|title=Meeting Notes Paris|url=http://www.humiliationstudies.org/documents/MeetingNotesParis04.pdf|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Humiliation Studies|language=en-US}}</ref> 
* National Headquarters of the [[United Methodist Church]], Washington, D.C.
* [[Harvard]], [[Stanford]], [[Yale]], and [[Princeton University|Princeton]] universities{{citation needed|date=May 2021}}

Fuller maintained a blog at the Breaking Ranks website,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Weblog|url=http://www.breakingranks.net/weblog/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Breaking Ranks|language=en-US}}</ref> and he also wrote regular articles for ''The Huffington Post''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Robert Fuller|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/robert-fuller|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Huffington Post|language=en-US}}</ref> and ''[[Psychology Today]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Somebodies and Nobodies|url=http://www.psychologytoday.com/blog/somebodies-and-nobodies|access-date=2021-05-01|website=Psychology Today|language=en-US}}</ref>

He explored the concepts of dignity and of dignitarian governance in his ''The Rowan Tree: A Novel'' (2013).<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Rowan Tree: A Novel|url=https://www.rowantreenovel.com|access-date=2021-05-01|website=The Rowan Tree: A Novel|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Fuller lived in [[Berkeley, California]], with his wife, Claire Sheridan. He had been married to Ann Lackritz Fuller and later to Alia Johnson. He had four children and four grandchildren. Fuller died on July 15, 2025, at the age of 88.<ref name=roberts>{{citation |last=Roberts |first=Sam |title=Robert W. Fuller, Who Championed Dignity Over 'Rankism,' Dies at 88| newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 25, 2025 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/25/books/robert-w-fuller-dead.html}}</ref>{{sfnb|Family|2025}}
